pronunciation_notes: mau at the end is known to mean 'place of'
cultural_notes: Woccon/Waccamaw people have been documented under many historical names since 1521
First recorded as Guacaya by Francisco Gordillo in 1521
Also called 'Northward's Indians' and 'Parched Corn Indians' in 1700s sources
Tom King was identified as a 'Woccon Indian' in William Byrd's writings
Historical documentation spans from 1521 to 1795 across multiple European sources
Name variations include Wococon, Wokakon, Wacawn, Woccoa, Wattomas, Waccamaw, and many others
Documentation sources include Spanish explorers, English colonists, maps, colonial records, and modern tribal sources
Woccon belonged to the Siouan linguistic stock, their closest relations being the Catawba
The Woccon primarily lived between Neuse River and one of its affluents, near present-day Goldsboro, Wayne County, North Carolina
First mention of the Woccon appears to be by Lawson writing about 1701, who recorded 150 words of their language
Lawson's vocabulary showed Woccon was nearer Catawba than any other known variety of speech
Dr. Douglas L. Rights theorized they were originally the Waccamaw tribe in southeastern North Carolina and northeastern South Carolina
Woccon took part against the whites in the Tuscarora Wars (1711-1715) and were probably extinguished as a tribe at that time
Remnants fled north with the Tuscarora, united with the Catawba, or combined with other Siouan remnants in the people later known as Croatan
Mooney estimated 600 Woccon in 1600, Lawson gives 120 warriors in 1701
Woccon is the only southern group of eastern Siouan tribes other than the Catawba from which a vocabulary has been preserved
Villages included Tooptatmeer and Yupwauremau, supposed to have been in Greene County
Spanish entrance in 1521 moved lots of tribes around and is believed to have pushed Waccamaw northwards
Francisco Gordillo possibly labeled the Waccamaw as the Guacaya in 1521, taking 150 captives from the area
Woccon people were encountered by Francisco Gordillo in 1521 along the Waccamaw and Pee Dee Rivers
Woccon appeared on the 1606 Hondius-Mercator Map as located at Ocracoke Island
The name Waccamaw was used by 1670, with English sources saying they lived along Waccamaw and PeeDee Rivers
Woccon people bounced around between North and South Carolina often due to Spanish entrada disruption in 16th-17th centuries
Woccon share significant ties with Cheraw/Saraw, Waccamaw of NC, Lumbee, Cape Fear, and Catawba tribes
Spanish colonization caused disease, enslavement, fear and mass migration affecting eastern seaboard nations
Many South Carolina tribes moved into the interior or up the coastline into North Carolina
Cape Fear Indians became 'Tribute Indians' by 1695 after constant attacks by natives allied with Charleston
In 1699, Richard Traunter described the 'Wacawn's' as 'Caniballs, and Maneaters'
William Hilton purchased land from Cape Fear Indians including from 'Wattcoosa' in 1663
John Lawson in 1701 recorded 120 fighting men and 500 inhabitants in two Woccon towns: Yupwareremau and Tooptatmeer
Lawson recorded 150 words of the Woccon language and identified it as Siouan stock
A group broke away from the main settlement and relocated southward according to Lawson's New Voyage to Carolina
Woccon participated in the Tuscarora War (1711-1713) as part of Captain Bull's Company in Barnwell's Army
Two Woccon were arrested in Virginia for leaving North Carolina without permission during the war period
The Woccon name disappears around the same time the Waccamaw name appears in historical records
Woccon were allied with other tribes including Watterees, Weneaws, Cape Fear, Wareperes, Saxapahaws, and Saraws in military campaigns
Historical documentation comes from Barnwell's military records and John Lawson's colonial observations
Waccamaw name first mentioned in 1712 when James Moore Jr. asked them and Cape Fears to join against the Tuscarora
Cape Fear people were known to be with the Woccon often
In 1715 Waccamaw had 610 people living near Winyaw of Pee Dee River
Waccamaw joined Yamassee and Cheraw in 1715 Yamassee War
Waccamaw attacked South Carolina on April 15, 1715 along with other native nations
Maurice Moore attacked and defeated Waccamaw in 1715, many were taken captive/enslaved
1715 head count showed 4 towns and 610 people between Waccamaw and Pee Dee Rivers
Trading houses were established at Winyaw and later Uauenee/Your Enee/Yahaunnah to trade with Waccamaw
Waccamaw Chiefs visited Charleston in Fall 1717
By 1718 Waccamaw had moved to Black River area
1718 Waccamaw War resulted in 60 killed or taken prisoner
By 1718 Waccamaw were living between Black and Sampit Rivers at Winyah Bay with 100 fighting men
Historical documentation comes from sources like John Swanton's Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin of 1952 and McDowell's records
Waccamaw town of several hundred people operated independently with own headman and fields
Waccamaw cooperated with Catawba nation but maintained independence
Some Waccamaw confederated with Catawba due to raids and enslavement by Seneca, Cherokee, and other groups
In 1723 some Waccamaw sought refuge with Winyaw and Pedee peoples
In 1723 Waccamaw petitioned to live on public land that used to belong to their ancestors
1725 Herbert Map shows Waccamaw largely in North Carolina on Lumber River
King Roger Moore's 1725 attacks on Cape Fear Indians forced them south to Winyah Bay area, affecting Waccamaw
In 1727 a Catawba leader reported that Waccamaw leader 'regards me not', showing Waccamaw independence
Waccamaw village was located half mile from Catawba leader's village in 1727
Mooney (1894) believes Waccamaw were finally incorporated with the Catawba
Alternative theory suggests Waccamaw were absorbed by English settlements rather than joining Catawba
1727 Upper House Journal of SC reports Waccamaw live near Catawba
By 1728/1733 Waccamaw are reported in Low Country of South Carolina
Waccamaw people were still present in parts of SC and NC as of 1734
By 1734, there were scarce Cape Fear or Waccamaw people who could give account of old inhabited areas
In 1741, Waccamaw were listed in Weaipee Town (Catawba area) with headmen receiving commissions from English
War broke out between Waccommassus (Waccamaw) and SC in 1749
In 1751, Waccamaw were described as 'one of the small friendly tribes' that SC wanted to be at peace with Iroquois
By 1755, Waccamaw were being called 'Settlement Indians' - this was the last reference to the name 'Waccamaw'
In 1778, many Waccamaw fled to NC swamps when SC Council made provisions for their protection
Dimery was in Drowning Creek Community (modern Robeson County NC) from 1780-1795
The Dimery family line can be traced through land purchases and census records from 1795-1850
Dimery Church was formed in 1878, eventually becoming Bethel Missionary Baptist
Multiple miscegenation cases involving tribal members occurred in early 1900s
Pine Level School (Dimery School) was founded in 1908 and classified as an Indian/'Special' School in 1922
The modern Waccamaw-Siouan tribe was formed in 1992 with initial organizational meeting on Oct. 17th
Woccon was most closely related to Catawba within the Siouan linguistic family
Woccon is part of the Eastern Siouan branch, along with Catawba
Western Siouan includes Dakota, Ofo, Tutelo, Biloxi, etc.
Woccon is a dormant Eastern Siouan language
The Woccon language closely resembled Catawba and was considered one of two Catawban languages
Waccon was a subdivision of the Waccamaw
Waccamaw territory was from Winyah Bay up Waccamaw River to the Cape Fear, and somewhat to the Neuse River
The tribe received recognition in 2005
HR1942 was signed in 2021
John Lawson documented a vocabulary of Woccon in 1709 in 'A New Voyage to Carolina'
Blair A. Rudes studied Woccon number words in 1985
Modern language revitalization efforts are documented by Passmore, Sayers, Bradley, and Lomboy in 2024
Woccon language phonology and morphology has been reconstituted by linguist B.A. Rudes
Woccon is classified as a coastal Catawban language
Woccon language data comes from historical sources including Colonial Records of North Carolina and South Carolina
John Lawson's 1709 'A New Voyage to Carolina' contains Woccon language documentation
Woccon people were documented in Tuscarora Expedition letters by Colonel John Barnwell
Historical records of Woccon people found in South Carolina Indian Trade Commission journals from 1710-1718
Woccon language has genetic affiliations studied by R. Carter in 1980
Woccon people were part of Carolina Lowland tribes along with Pedee, Sewee, Winyaw, Waccamaw, Cape Fear, Congaree, Wateree, and Santee
Woccon is documented in Colonial Records of South Carolina from 1710-1718
Woccon is classified as a Siouan tribe of the Carolinas according to Frank G. Speck's 1935 research
Woccon documentation exists in British Public Record Office records relating to South Carolina from 1663-1770
Woccon is known from Catawba, Tutelo, and documentary sources according to Speck's anthropological work
